must_find.item: Women survived at a much higher rate than men (about 74% against 19%).
must_find.quote: Survival rates for the four groups (Male/Female x Pclass 1/2/3) are: Female in 1st Class (96.8%), Male in 1st Class (36.9%), Female in 2nd Class (92.1%), Male in 2nd Class (15.7%), Female in 3rd Class (50.4%), Male in 3rd Class (13.6%).
must_find.reason: Report gives female vs male rates by class and a significant Sex chi-square, but never states overall women vs men rates (74% vs 19%) directly; the per-class numbers imply it and show direction.

must_find.item: Survival falls with passenger class, highest in first class and lowest in third.
must_find.quote: survival rates varied significantly by passenger class, with first-class passengers having a much higher survival probability than third-class.
must_find.reason: States direction: first class higher than third.

must_find.item: Passengers who survived had paid higher fares on average.
must_find.quote: For Fare, the t-test shows a highly significant difference in survival rates ($t = 6.84$, $p = 2.70e-11$)
must_find.reason: Fare significance is reported, and survivor mean fares are higher within each sex ($40.82 vs $21.96 for males), showing direction.

must_find.item: Passengers without a recorded cabin survived less often than those with one.
must_find.quote: Passengers with missing 'Cabin' data have a survival rate of 0.300, compared to 0.667 for those with recorded cabin values (p-value: 3.09e-22).
must_find.reason: Directly states lower survival for missing cabin.

must_find.item: Passengers with a missing Age survived less often than those with a recorded Age.
must_find.quote: Passengers with missing 'Age' data have a survival rate of 0.294, compared to 0.406 for those with recorded age values (p-value: 0.0059).
must_find.reason: Directly states lower survival for missing age.

must_find.item: A predictive model is compared with the majority-class baseline (about 62% accuracy) and beats it.
must_find.quote: significantly outperforming a baseline model that predicted the most frequent class (~59%).
must_find.reason: Compares models with majority-class baseline and beats it, though baseline is ~59% rather than ~62%.

must_find.item: Model results include precision, recall or F1, not only accuracy.
must_find.quote: The Logistic Regression model achieved a test accuracy of 0.8101, also outperforming the baseline.
must_find.reason: Only accuracy is reported; no precision, recall or F1.

must_not_claim.quote: Approximately 61.6% of passengers did not survive ('Survived'=0), while approximately 38.4% survived
must_not_claim.reason: Report states most did not survive, the opposite.

must_not_claim.item: Men survived at a higher rate than women.
must_not_claim.reason: Report shows women surviving more than men in every class.

must_not_claim.item: Third-class passengers survived at a higher rate than first-class passengers.
must_not_claim.quote: first-class passengers having a much higher survival probability than third-class
must_not_claim.reason: States the opposite of the claim.

must_not_claim.item: Age is the strongest predictor of survival.
must_not_claim.quote: The Random Forest model identifies 'Sex', 'Fare', and 'Age' as the top three features driving survival predictions, with importance scores of 0.2733, 0.2721, and 0.2527 respectively.
must_not_claim.reason: Age is listed third, not strongest; report says Age is a weaker association.

caveats.quote: Missing data patterns reveal that missing 'Cabin' records are strongly associated with lower passenger classes and non-survival
caveats.reason: Cabin missingness is discussed extensively and is associated with class and survival, though not framed explicitly as a limitation.
